title: ILGC Project: Cyclorotor Autogyro
text: ←Apurv Bhushan

title: ILGC Project: Cyclorotor Autogyro
text:
Project Overview and Research Basis
In a motorized cyclorotor, blades rotate around a central axis while changing pitch cyclically; adjusting the pitch offset can redirect the rotor’s thrust whereas a fixed-pitch cyclorotor produces thrust in a single direction. The project explores using a fixed-pitch cyclorotor as the main lift-generating rotor on an autogyro aircraft, with the goal of developing a physical prototype and investigating the concept through design, simulation, and experiments.
The idea is motivated by the research paper Energetic Design of a New Autogyro Aircraft with Cyclorotors with Possibility of Energy Harvesting. It proposes an aircraft with two cylindrical cyclorotor wind turbines mounted on either side of the fuselage, and estimates aerodynamic and vehicle quantities mathematically. As described in my project log, the concept had not yet been demonstrated with a physical aircraft. My aim is to develop a physical cyclorotor-autogyro prototype and investigate the concept through design, simulation, and experiments.

Testing the First Rotary Kite: The “Rola-Rola” (also known online as the UFO)

The first physical experiment in this project was a rotary kite known as the Rola-Rola, or the UFO. I am fascinated by how it flies: two pieces of Depron foam are joined perpendicular to one another, with spars, strings, and threads supporting the structure. In flight, the rectangular horizontal plate rotates around an axis along its length, producing a surprisingly simple but intriguing flying mechanism.

Makerspace on Wheels
Inspired by the idea of Science on Wheels, Makerspace on Wheels brings hands-on making to government-school students. The van would travel to schools across the country, giving students the chance to learn by building, experimenting, and using practical tools.

title: CANSAT 2026-27
text:
Project Overview
CanSat is an international aerospace engineering competition in which student teams design, build, and test a miniature satellite (CanSat) that simulates the functions of a real satellite within the dimensions of a soft-drink can.
The 2027 mission involves deploying a 2P PocketQube from the CanSat at 90% of its peak altitude, followed by autonomous descent at a target velocity of (10 ) m/s. The PocketQube must power up upon release, deploy two solar panels after a 5-second delay, and demonstrate successful deployment through onboard sensing and telemetry.

title: Hello! My name is Apurv Bhushan

title: Summer Internship 2026
text:
The Sheldahl and Klimas Dataset
Sheldahl and Klimas (1981) report wind-tunnel measurements of symmetric NACA airfoils across angles of attack and Reynolds numbers. The digitized collection includes lift, drag, moment, and axial-force coefficients, along with lift-drag polars and increasing/decreasing angle-of-attack sweeps.

title: Summer Internship 2026
text:
Digitization Process
I loaded the scanned plots into WebPlotDigitizer and selected a 2D XY plot. I calibrated the axes by marking four known reference points and entering their values; for example, the NACA 0015 full-range lift plot uses an angle-of-attack range of 0 to 180 degrees and a lift-coefficient range of -1.2 to 1.2.
I then extracted each curve using manual point selection or color-based automatic extraction, checked the traced points against the plotted curves, and exported the results as CSV files. The included MATLAB scripts organize and plot the digitized series for comparison.

Process Screenshots




Step 1: Load the source graph image into WebPlotDigitizer.





Step 2: Choose a 2D XY axes type.





Step 3: Mark the four reference points used to calibrate the axes.





Step 4: Enter the known minimum and maximum values for each axis.

title: Summer Internship 2026
section: CFD Simulations for the Cyclorotor Autogyro
text:
CFD Simulations for the Cyclorotor Autogyro
After completing the airfoil-data work, I moved on to CFD simulations of a flat plate for my Cyclorotor Autogyro project. The project explores whether a cyclorotor could provide lift for an autogyro aircraft, with a physical prototype as the longer-term goal.
I would also like to credit Professor Shashikant Pawar for his help with the CFD simulations. He is also a mentor for my passion project.
The project log notes that flat plates can be a more suitable starting point than symmetrical airfoils at low Reynolds numbers. I began with flat-plate simulations to study the airflow and build a foundation for the project’s later design and physical experiments.

Internship Overview
During my first-year summer, I worked in Plaksha University’s Makerspace on two projects. I spent a few days building a variable voltage power supply using a 220 V-to-30 V transformer and a buck converter. Most of my internship, about 95%, went toward designing and building a motorized cyclorotor.

title: Plaksha Makerspace Internship
text:
Cyclorotor Project
A cyclorotor is a rotor whose blades revolve around a central axis while changing their pitch during each rotation. This lets the rotor generate and redirect thrust, making it possible to control the direction of the force without turning the whole assembly. My project involved designing and building a working cyclorotor assembly.



Prototype 1: the first physical cyclorotor prototype.





Airfoil rib structure used in the rotor assembly.

title: Plaksha Makerspace Internship
text:
What I Learned
This was my first substantial mechanical design project, and it taught me how much work remains between a computer model and a reliable physical assembly. I encountered unwanted friction in joints, challenges fitting and assembling components, and the need to think carefully about clearances and fastening methods. My initial fastening designs were not as refined as they needed to be, but working through those issues gave me valuable practical experience in mechanical design, prototyping, and iteration.

title: Optimization Course Project
text:
Project Overview
For my third-semester Optimization course, my team developed AdaGamma, an extension of Adam that uses gradient skewness and kurtosis to modulate parameter updates. We tested it against established optimizers on quadratic functions, the Rosenbrock function, and MNIST digit classification.

text:
Project Log

title: Optimization Course Project
text:
What I Learned

I developed a deeper understanding of how the first four gradient moments relate to an optimizer’s update, and how skewness and kurtosis can be used to adjust it.
I worked on the mathematical design, translating the update rule into an implementation, and tuning hyperparameters across benchmark problems.
I learned that an optimizer’s performance depends on the task: AdaGamma converged faster on the tested quadratic and Rosenbrock functions, but on MNIST it achieved accuracy similar to Adam while taking longer to train. This reinforced the importance of evaluating optimization methods across different kinds of problems.
